```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.height = 4,
                      fig.width = 7)
set.seed(2021)
```

```{r sim1}
library(occAssess)
```

### Introduction

This vignette demonstrates the main occurrence-data functions in
<code>occAssess</code> using only datasets distributed with the package. It is
executed when the package vignettes are built and requires no downloads or
local files.

### Occurrence data 

In this worked example, I simulated data for 11 species across the UK. The species were simulated with varying prevalence (number of records drawn from a uniform distribution between 500 and 1500) and randomly over the period 2001 to 2010. The data were generated as weighted random samples across space (WGS84 coordinate reference system), where the weights were taken from a separate species distribution modelling exercises. Each simulated data point was randomly assigned to one of two surveys which are specified in the "identifier" field. The data can be accessed within occAssess as follows:


```{r sim2}

data("simDat")

spDat <- simDat

str(spDat)

```

### Periods

In this example, we specify five two-year periods covering 2001 to 2010.


```{r sim3}

periods <- list(2001:2002, 2003:2004, 2005:2006, 2007:2008, 2009:2010)
```

### Temporally uncertain observations

All period-based functions use one temporal-assignment implementation. Date
bounds describe uncertainty about when one observation occurred; they do not
mean continuous observation and never cause a row to be copied into several
periods. Intervals wholly contained in a period are assigned automatically.
Ambiguous intervals are dropped by default, while optional allocation rules can
assign each to one period.

This small example combines an exact-year fallback, a range within one period,
a range crossing a boundary, an end-only record, and an exact ISO date encoded
as equal bounds.

```{r uncertain-dates}
uncertainDat <- data.frame(
  species = rep("example species", 5),
  x = 1:5,
  y = 1:5,
  year = c(1995, NA, NA, NA, NA),
  startDate = c(NA, "2002", "1999", NA, "2005-06-14"),
  endDate = c(NA, "2007", "2003", "2005", "2005-06-14"),
  spatialUncertainty = 0,
  identifier = "survey"
)
uncertainPeriods <- list(1990:1999, 2000:2009)

dropDates <- suppressWarnings(assessRecordNumber(
  dat = uncertainDat,
  species = "species", x = "x", y = "y", year = "year",
  spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty", identifier = "identifier",
  periods = uncertainPeriods,
  dateHandling = list(start = "startDate", end = "endDate")
))

overlapDates <- suppressWarnings(assessRecordNumber(
  dat = uncertainDat,
  species = "species", x = "x", y = "y", year = "year",
  spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty", identifier = "identifier",
  periods = uncertainPeriods,
  dateHandling = list(
    start = "startDate", end = "endDate",
    ambiguous = "maxOverlap", endOnly = "earliest"
  )
))

dropDates$data
overlapDates$data
attr(overlapDates, "temporalDiagnostics")
```

`maxOverlap` is a pragmatic allocation rule, not an estimate of the true date.
Using `start`, `end`, `earliest`, or `latest` can shift apparent trends towards
earlier or later periods. Analysts should choose and report a rule appropriate
to their data, and can inspect the `temporalDiagnostics` attribute to see how
many records were assigned or excluded.

### Functions

The functions below use the occurrence data and periods defined above. Most
return a named list containing the numerical result and a ggplot object; consult
the individual help pages because exact component names and structures vary.

#### assessRecordNumber

<code>assessRecordNumber()</code> counts records per period and identifier. For
the functions that accept configurable column names, the <code>species</code>,
<code>x</code>, <code>y</code>, <code>year</code>,
<code>spatialUncertainty</code>, and <code>identifier</code> arguments identify
the corresponding columns in <code>dat</code>.


```{r sim4}

nRec <- assessRecordNumber(dat = spDat,
                           periods = periods,
                           species = "species",
                           x = "x",
                           y = "y",
                           year = "year", 
                           spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty",
                           identifier = "identifier")


nRec$plot
```

This function enables researchers to quickly establish how the number of records has changed over time. 

#### assessSpeciesNumber 

In addition to the number of records, you may wish to know how the number of species (taxonomic coverage) in your dataset changes over time. For this you can use the function assessSpeciesNumber:


```{r sim5}

nSpec <- assessSpeciesNumber(dat = spDat,
                           periods = periods,
                           species = "species",
                           x = "x",
                           y = "y",
                           year = "year", 
                           spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty",
                           identifier = "identifier")

nSpec$plot
```

#### assessSpeciesID 

It has been speculated that apparent changes in taxonomic coverage could, in fact, reflect a change in taxonomic expertise over time. For example, if fewer individuals have the skill to identify certain species, then it may not appear in your dataset in the later periods. The function assessSpeciesID treats the proportion of records identified to species level as a proxy for taxonomic expertise: 


```{r sim6}

propID <- assessSpeciesID(dat = spDat,
                           periods = periods,
                           type = "proportion",
                           species = "species",
                           x = "x",
                           y = "y",
                           year = "year", 
                           spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty",
                           identifier = "identifier")

propID$plot + ggplot2::ylim(c(0,1)) ## it is easy to modify the outputs of the functions in occAssess to e.g. change axis ranges
```

The argument "type" can take the values proportion (proportion of records identified to species level) or count (number of records identified to species level). 

#### assessSpatialUncertainty

<code>assessSpatialUncertainty()</code> uses the package's standard column
names. It plots the non-missing uncertainty values by period and returns, for
each identifier, the proportion of retained records for which spatial
uncertainty is specified. That proportion is pooled across all selected
periods; records with missing uncertainty remain in its denominator.

```{r sim-spatial-uncertainty}
spatUncertainty <- assessSpatialUncertainty(
  dat = spDat,
  periods = periods
)

spatUncertainty$data
spatUncertainty$plot
```

#### assessRarityBias

<code>assessRarityBias()</code> measures association between recorded range
size (the number of occupied grid cells) and record count. With
<code>metric = "r2"</code>, the index is the coefficient of determination from
the period-specific regression; <code>metric = "cor"</code> requests Pearson
correlation. When <code>prevPerPeriod = TRUE</code>, occupied cells are
calculated separately in each period. When it is <code>FALSE</code>, each
species' occupied cells are calculated across all selected periods. At least
five species are required for an identifier-period estimate.


```{r sim7}

taxBias <- assessRarityBias(dat = spDat,
                            periods = periods,
                            res = 0.5,
                            prevPerPeriod = FALSE,
                            species = "species",
                            x = "x",
                            y = "y",
                            year = "year", 
                            spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty",
                            identifier = "identifier",
                            returnDiagnostics = TRUE,
                            plotRegressions = TRUE,
                            labelTopResiduals = 2)

taxBias$data

taxBias$plot + ggplot2::ylim(c(0,1))
```

The optional summaries expose the untransformed OLS models underpinning that
time series. Positive residuals have more records than fitted conditional on
their occupied-cell count; negative residuals have fewer. They are exploratory
diagnostics, not significance tests or proof that a species is genuinely over-
or under-sampled.

```{r rarity-diagnostics}
taxBias$regressionDiagnostics

raritySpecies <- taxBias$speciesDiagnostics
finiteResiduals <- raritySpecies[is.finite(raritySpecies$residual), ]

# Largest positive and negative residuals
head(finiteResiduals[order(-finiteResiduals$residual),
                     c("identifier", "period", "species", "residual")])
head(finiteResiduals[order(finiteResiduals$residual),
                     c("identifier", "period", "species", "residual")])

# One customisable, period-faceted plot per identifier
taxBias$regressionPlots[[1]]
```

With `prevPerPeriod = FALSE`, occupied-cell counts are calculated across all
selected periods while record counts remain period-specific. Setting it to
`TRUE` estimates occupied cells separately in each period. Occupied-cell count
is only a proxy for commonness and is estimated from the same recording process
as record count. Consequently, a strong fitted relationship does not establish
unbiased sampling, and highly recorded or influential species can materially
affect the line.

#### assessSpatialCov 

<code>assessSpatialCov()</code> grids records at a specified resolution and maps
them in geographic space. These coordinates are WGS84 longitude/latitude, so
country borders can be requested with <code>countries = "UK"</code>. The
function returns one ggplot object per identifier; density output is faceted by
period.


```{r sim8}

map <- assessSpatialCov(dat = spDat,
                        periods = periods,
                        res = 0.5,
                        logCount = TRUE,
                        countries = "UK",
                        species = "species",
                        x = "x",
                        y = "y",
                        year = "year", 
                        spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty",
                        identifier = "identifier")

map$survey1
```


```{r sim9}

map$survey2
```

<code>res</code> is expressed in the units of the occurrence coordinates
(decimal degrees here, or typically metres for a projected CRS).
<code>logCount</code> applies a base-10 transformation to density displays and
returned density rasters, but not to sampled-period or overlap calculations.
The <code>countries</code> borders come from
<code>ggplot2::map_data("world")</code> and are appropriate only for WGS84
longitude/latitude. For projected or custom study regions, supply a compatible
spatial polygon object through <code>shp</code> instead.


#### assessSpatialBias

<code>assessSpatialBias()</code> compares the empirical mean nearest-neighbour
distance with distances from random samples drawn inside a raster mask. Values
below one indicate greater clustering than the random samples; values above one
indicate greater dispersion. The mask must be numeric inside the sampling domain
and <code>NA</code> outside it, and must use the same CRS as the occurrence
coordinates. A compatible UK mask is bundled for this example.


```{r sim10}

data("UKWGS84mask")

UKWGS84mask

```


```{r sim11}

spatBias <- assessSpatialBias(dat = spDat,
                              periods = periods,
                              mask = UKWGS84mask,
                              nSamps = 10,
                              degrade = TRUE,
                              species = "species",
                              x = "x",
                              y = "y",
                              year = "year", 
                              spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty",
                              identifier = "identifier")

str(spatBias$data)

spatBias$plot + ggplot2::ylim(c(0, 2.15)) # ylim set to theoretical range of possible values for the nearest neighbour index
```

<code>nSamps</code> controls the number of random samples. Because this step is
stochastic, the setup chunk calls <code>set.seed(2021)</code> to make the
vignette reproducible. With <code>degrade = TRUE</code>, duplicate coordinate
pairs are removed within each period and identifier. The ribbon shows the 5th
and 95th percentiles across the random-sample comparisons.

#### assessEnvBias 

<code>assessEnvBias()</code> uses principal components to display occurrences
in environmental space. The bundled <code>simEnvDat</code> rows correspond
one-for-one, in the same order, with <code>simDat</code>;
<code>backgroundEnvDat</code> is a separate sample of background environmental
space. Both tables contain the same environmental columns. They were derived
from WorldClim variables; current source data are available from
[WorldClim](https://www.worldclim.org/).


```{r sim12}

data("simEnvDat") # climate data at locations of simulated occurrence data

data("backgroundEnvDat") # climate data at 4000 random locations across the UK
```
With background data supplied, the PCA is fitted to the background and the
occurrence rows are projected onto those axes. Without background data, a
separate PCA is fitted to each identifier's complete, retained occurrence rows.
Rows removed by spatial-uncertainty filtering remain paired with their matching
environmental rows.


```{r sim13}

envBias <- assessEnvBias(dat = spDat,
                         periods = periods,
                         envDat = simEnvDat,
                         backgroundEnvDat = backgroundEnvDat,
                         xPC = 1,
                         yPC = 2,
                         species = "species",
                         x = "x",
                         y = "y",
                         year = "year", 
                         spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty",
                         identifier = "identifier")

envBias$plot
```

The arguments yPC and xPC indicate which principal components you would like on the y and x axes, respectively. 

#### assessEnvCoverage

<code>assessEnvCoverage()</code> complements the PCA display above by fitting a
kernel density to each period's occurrence environments in one common
background-based, standardised PCA space. For each probability-mass
highest-density region (HDR), it reports the proportion of the supplied
reference observations inside the fitted region. The following compact example
uses a broad environmental sample in the first period and a more restricted
sample in the second.

```{r environmental-coverage}
coverageBackground <- expand.grid(
  temperature = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 9),
  rainfall = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 9)
)

broadRows <- c(1, 5, 9, 19, 25, 33, 41, 49, 57, 65, 73, 77, 81)
restrictedRows <- c(31, 32, 33, 40, 41, 42, 49, 50, 51, 39, 43, 30, 52)
coverageEnv <- coverageBackground[c(broadRows, restrictedRows), ]
coverageDat <- data.frame(
  species = "example species",
  x = seq_len(nrow(coverageEnv)),
  y = seq_len(nrow(coverageEnv)),
  year = rep(c(2001, 2003), each = length(broadRows)),
  spatialUncertainty = 0,
  identifier = "survey"
)

envCoverage <- assessEnvCoverage(
  dat = coverageDat,
  species = "species", x = "x", y = "y", year = "year",
  spatialUncertainty = "spatialUncertainty", identifier = "identifier",
  periods = list(2001:2002, 2003:2004),
  envDat = coverageEnv,
  backgroundEnvDat = coverageBackground,
  hdrProbs = c(0.50, 0.80, 0.95),
  bandwidth = diag(c(0.30, 0.30)),
  gridSize = 101
)

envCoverage$data[, c("period", "hdrProbability", "backgroundCoverage",
                     "nSample", "status")]
envCoverage$plot
```

The fixed bandwidth makes this small demonstration exactly reproducible; when
it is omitted, one plug-in bandwidth is estimated from all retained occurrence
scores and reused across periods. HDR levels are probability masses under the
sample KDE, not percentages of its maximum height. Multiple rows at the same
location or sampling unit influence the KDE, so any scientifically justified
aggregation should be performed before the function is called.

Coverage is conditional on how the reference environment was sampled and on
the bandwidth, sample size, selected PCA axes, and sampling unit. Uniform
longitude-latitude raster cells do not necessarily represent equal land area,
and two PCA axes need not capture all environmental differences. High coverage
therefore does not establish unbiased sampling, while low coverage is not by
itself evidence of a causal selection process. This implementation adapts the
KDE/HDR environmental-coverage idea explored in
[npmsEnvBiasChecks](https://github.com/sacrevert/npmsEnvBiasChecks) without its
project-specific clustering or data dependencies.

#### assessBias1D

<code>assessBias1D()</code> compares the distribution of one variable among
sampled units with its distribution across a reference population. The optional
metrics table reports total variation distance (TV) and mean absolute error
(MAE) before and after weighting. This synthetic example has known population
proportions of 0.2, 0.1, 0.4, and 0.3, while the unweighted sample proportions
are 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4.

```{r one-dimensional-bias}
biasPopulation <- data.frame(
  environment = rep(1:4, c(20, 10, 40, 30)),
  sampled = 0L
)
sampledRows <- c(1, 21:22, 31:33, 71:74)
biasPopulation$sampled[sampledRows] <- 1L

# These row-aligned weights give the sampled units total bin weights
# proportional to the reference-population distribution.
calibrationWeights <- numeric(nrow(biasPopulation))
calibrationWeights[sampledRows] <- rep(
  c(0.20, 0.05, 4 / 30, 0.075),
  c(1, 2, 3, 4)
)

bias1D <- assessBias1D(
  pop = biasPopulation,
  R = "sampled",
  x = "environment",
  weights = calibrationWeights,
  breaks = c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5),
  RNames = "survey",
  WNames = "calibrated",
  returnMetrics = TRUE
)

bias1D$metrics
bias1D$plot
```

The unweighted comparison has TV 0.2 and MAE 0.1. Here the illustrative
weights exactly reproduce the reference bin proportions, so both weighted
metrics are zero. In general, weighting can either reduce or increase the
discrepancy. For <code>K</code> bins, <code>MAE = 2 * TV / K</code>, so these
are related summaries rather than independent evidence. Both depend on the
reference population, variable, bin boundaries, missing-value treatment, and
weights. They describe discrete binned distributions and are not formal tests
or universal estimates of sampling bias.
